title: Visiting the sick
hook: the Talmud says a visitor takes away a sixtieth of the illness (Nedarim 39b)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was giyur, conversion, and your line was a new name. Whose chosen name did you honor? Today, a commandment anyone can do with a pair of shoes and an hour. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

One sixtieth. That's the claim, in the Talmud, tractate Nedarim: whoever visits a sick person takes away a sixtieth of the illness. The rabbis around the table hear it and do the math out loud. Then sixty visitors should cure him completely? They don't laugh it off, and they don't take it literally. They add conditions and keep going. Nobody in the conversation says the visit is pointless. The argument is only about how much it carries. Today is that visit: the mitzvah of visiting the sick.
screen: `ONE SIXTIETH.` → `THEN SIXTY VISITORS?` → `THE VISIT CARRIES SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew it's bikur cholim, visiting the sick. Turn it four ways. First, where it starts. In Genesis, Abraham is recovering from his circumcision, sitting at the opening of his tent, and the text says the Lord appeared to him there. The Talmud reads that as God visiting the sick, and draws a line: as God visits the sick, so should you. Visiting is walking in God's ways. Second, a story. On the same page in Nedarim, a student of Rabbi Akiva falls ill and nobody comes. Akiva goes himself. The floor is swept and sprinkled for the sick man, he recovers, and the student says, Rabbi, you have brought me back to life. Akiva walks out and teaches: anyone who does not visit the sick is like one who sheds blood. Strong words, said to make a point: absence costs something. Third, how. Later teachers give practical advice. Don't stay so long you exhaust the person. Sit at their level, not looming over the bed. Ask what they need: the floor swept, the groceries, the dog walked. Fourth, why you go. The visit is also for prayer. The tradition says to pray for the sick person while you are with them, because you see their need with your own eyes. There's a short line people say: may God have mercy on you among all the sick of Israel. Even the prayer refuses to leave anyone alone. A sixtieth is small. It is not nothing. Visiting lightens.
screen: `GOD VISITED ABRAHAM.` · `AKIVA GOES HIMSELF.` · `SHORT VISITS, LOW CHAIRS.` · `PRAY WHERE YOU CAN SEE.` · then, large: `VISITING LIGHTENS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit someone unwell. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is sick or stuck at home right now: a relative, a neighbor, a coworker on leave. Breathe in, and see where they are sitting today. Breathe out, and ask what they might need that isn't advice. Then plan the visit, small and real. A call, a doorstep drop-off, a short visit in a low chair. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Visiting the sick. Bikur cholim: the way God visited Abraham, Akiva at a lonely student's bedside, a short visit, and a prayer at the bedside. Today's word.
Your line: visiting lightens. Today, take one sixtieth off someone's load: a visit, a call, or one errand they can't run themselves. Day one thousand three hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Visiting the sick, bikur cholim, is a commandment and an act of kindness in Jewish life; some synagogues have a bikur cholim group that organizes visits, calls, meals and errands for members who are ill or homebound.

fork.setup: you're Rabbi Akiva. one of your students is sick, and nobody has come to see him. what do you do?
options: send word that he should be patient.
wait for someone else to go.
fork.reveal: Akiva goes himself; the floor is swept and sprinkled for the student, and he says, you have brought me back to life.

trapdoor: what you thought: visiting the sick is just being polite.
what it means: a commandment, walking in God's ways, with practical rules and prayer at the bedside.
what a scholar hears: Nedarim 39b–40a's sixtieth and Akiva's student, and Sotah 14a reading Genesis 18 as God visiting the sick.

notes: Nedarim 39b (a visitor removes a sixtieth; the 'sixty visitors' objection and its qualifications) paraphrased; confirm the summary 'they add conditions'.
Nedarim 40a (Akiva's student; 'you have revived me'; whoever does not visit is like one who sheds blood) paraphrased; confirm.
Sotah 14a (God visited the sick, Genesis 18:1) paraphrased; confirm.
Practical advice (not too long, sit at their level, pray in their presence) drawn from Nedarim 40a and Shulchan Aruch YD 335; confirm.
Prayer line 'may God (HaMakom) have mercy on you among all the sick of Israel' (Shabbat 12b) described, not quoted; confirm wording.
howItsDone 'some synagogues have a bikur cholim group' — confirm.
